Onboarding: It's Not How Many Hours of Induction You Give, but How Clear the Job Becomes

LinkedIn article by Benito López Ramírez

In my previous lives (that's what I call my experience working at different companies), I've seen both good and bad onboarding practices.

When it's done well, within the right timeframe, with experts involved and a clear structure, the results are impressive.

But I've also seen the opposite: people who went through many hours of induction and, even so, arrived at their position not knowing how to carry out their tasks.

Clarity is the foundation

Regardless of the area or position, every new team member needs to be clear on:

  • What their roles and responsibilities are.
  • Which applications and tools they will use.
  • Who their internal customers are and how they work with them.
  • What their deliverables and operational KPIs are.

An onboarding program can be very good and still fail in day-to-day work if the person isn't certain about what is expected of them.

This is where support comes in

We need to verify that what was “learned” in theory can be applied in practice. That the job description and standard work are clear and match what was covered in training.

And that the new team member understands the scope of their work and the importance of doing it well.

Adults learn by doing

Exams can be used, but what I've seen work best is putting knowledge into practice and having the instructor validate it.

Adults learn by doing, not by sitting for hours listening.

My takeaway: onboarding doesn't end when the training ends. It ends when the person can do their job with clarity and confidence.

And you, what onboarding practice has worked best in your company or team? Do you use digital tools or artificial intelligence to measure learning and follow up on what was taught?
